article.title: Indonesia Luxury Travel
article.author: Tiqua Jackson
article.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Once a year, the whole island of Bali goes silent for a day. Nyepi, the Balinese Hindu New Year, shuts the island down completely, airport included, and no hotel concierge can talk anyone onto a plane. A traveller who has paid for a cliff-top villa and a private driver can land on the wrong date and spend the night in a transit lounge somewhere else in Asia. Nyepi is the most dramatic of the planning errors that spoil expensive Indonesian trips, though quieter ones sit alongside it. Almost all can be avoided with a few decisions made early. How far apart are the islands? Few countries are as scattered. Some 6,000 inhabited islands sit among more than 17,000 in total, ringed by over 100,000 km of coastline, and the distance from Aceh at the tip of Sumatra to the far side of Papua is about 5,200 km. The usual first-draft itinerary of Bali and Raja Ampat in a week looks tidy on a screen. In practice it means early check-outs and a lot of time in departure halls. A better shape is two regions, each given room to breathe. Bali paired with Lombok, or Bali paired with the Komodo area of Flores, keeps the connections short. Indonesia luxury tours that plan around domestic flights and private transfers let the whole route run from one confirmed schedule, with each leg timed to the next. With ten days or more, a third region in the east becomes realistic, and Raja Ampat or Sumba then gets the time it deserves. Wet season sunshine is wishful thinking Java and Bali, like most of the country, are driest from April to October. Outside those months, afternoons often bring heavy downpours and boat days are more likely to be cancelled. A week of snorkelling and island-hopping booked for January is a gamble. That doesn't make the wet months a write-off. A slow stay in the hills around Ubud, built on spa treatments and cooking classes, suits the green, damp season well, and rain on a jungle canopy from a covered terrace is no hardship. Trips that depend on calm water and clear skies belong between April and October. Check the Nyepi date first Nyepi follows the Balinese calendar, so it moves each year and usually lands in March. On the day itself, the airport and seaports close, and hotels ask guests to stay on the property, with lights kept low after dark. The fix is simple. Look up the date before booking flights, and keep arrivals and departures well clear of it. Some travellers choose to be there for it. Arriving two days ahead means seeing the ogoh-ogoh parades the evening before, then spending a day of enforced stillness at a resort with nowhere to be. For a honeymoon, that can be the most memorable day of the trip. Look beyond Bali's airport Over half of all foreign tourists land at Bali's Ngurah Rai airport (DPS). That makes sense for a Bali-centred trip. It makes very little sense for one focused on Java or the outer islands, where routing everything back through Denpasar adds flights and nights. Flying into Jakarta and out of Bali, or the reverse, often saves a full day of doubling back. Who is running the trip? A bespoke itinerary across several islands is only as reliable as the people holding it together. Itineraries here shift at short notice: weather can cancel a ferry or close a port, and domestic flights get retimed without warning. Official travel advice recommends large, reputable agents for exactly this reason. Before paying a deposit, ask who rebooks a cancelled connection at night and whether there's a local office on the ground. A small agent found through a social media page may be charming, and may also go quiet when a boat doesn't sail. Is a yacht worth it? For the remote east, often yes. A liveaboard or private phinisi in the Komodo area or Raja Ampat turns long transfers into part of the holiday, with a cook and a crew that knows the anchorages. Arriving by private yacht is also more straightforward than many assume. A visit permit valid for 30 days needs only three days' notice, and it can be renewed once for another 30. For those who prefer a larger ship, cruises call at Benoa in Bali and Makassar in Sulawesi, among other ports. Leave room for the villa It's easy to pay for an infinity pool and never sit by it. Two nights per stop sounds efficient until each stay becomes a check-in and a packing session with a dinner squeezed between. Three or four nights at each place gives time for slow mornings and the afternoon nobody planned. Lazy days are the point of a high-end trip, and they need gaps in the schedule. Visas and clocks For most short trips, a visa on arrival or an e-visa is enough. It's valid for 30 days and can be extended once for another 30. Anyone staying longer than a month should arrange the extension before the first period runs out, and a reputable operator can usually help with the paperwork. Indonesia also spans three time zones, from UTC+7 in Java to UTC+9 in Papua, with Bali and Lombok on UTC+8. There's no daylight saving time. A flight from Bali to Jakarta lands an hour "earlier" on the clock, which matters when a private transfer is waiting. Booking confirmations should always show local time. Where to start First, pick the travel month and check it against the Nyepi date and the dry season. Second, choose two regions and the entry and exit airports that suit them, adding a yacht leg if the eastern islands are on the list. Third, shortlist an established operator and ask how they handle changes. Confirm visa length and time zones before the flights are ticketed.
